deep.reconstruction:
Setting (author's statement): segment AB has midpoint C, and the line MCN is perpendicular to AB at C, so MN is the perpendicular bisector of AB. Theorem (Lehrsatz): (a) every point of MN is equidistant from A and B; (b) every point not on MN is closer to A or to B, according as it lies on the same side of MN as A or as B.

Proof I (points on MN). If the point is C, then AC = CB by hypothesis. Otherwise call the point R and join it to A and B. In triangles ACR and BCR: AC = BC; the angles at C are equal, both right ('C = C'); CR is common. By SAS (Euclid I.4), AR = BR.

Proof II (point Q off MN, on A's side). Two subcases.
(i) Q lies on the line AB. If Q is beyond A (outside segment AC), then QB = QA + AB > QA. If Q is between C and A, then QB = BC + CQ = AC + CQ = (QA + QC) + CQ = QA + 2CQ > QA. [Mine: the step AC = AQ + QC is implicit.]
(ii) Q is not on line AB. Then segment BQ crosses MN at a point R, since Q and B are on opposite sides of MN. Join A to R. In triangle ABQ, R lies on side BQ, so ray AR lies inside angle BAQ. Hence angle BAQ = RAQ + BAR. By part I, AR = BR, so triangle ABR is isosceles and BAR = ABR [mine: Euclid I.5, not cited]. Since R lies on BQ, ABR = ABQ (the interlinear insertion '= RAQ + ABQ'). So BAQ = RAQ + ABQ > ABQ. In triangle ABQ the greater angle is opposite the greater side: BAQ is opposite BQ and ABQ is opposite AQ. Therefore BQ > AQ.

The case of Q on B's side follows by symmetry and is left implicit. The page has an accompanying figure. It is a careful Euclid-style school proof of the perpendicular-bisector characterization, with an exhaustive case split. It is unrelated to the spherical right-triangle formulas on the previous folio.
errors: Citation slip: the inference 'angle BAQ > angle ABQ, hence BQ > AQ' is Euclid I.19 (the greater angle is subtended by the greater side), not I.18, which is the converse.
Implicit step: BAR = ABR needs the isosceles base-angle theorem (Euclid I.5) applied to AR = BR from part I. It is not cited.

Unjustified (standard) step: that BQ actually meets MN, and that R lies between B and Q so that ray AR is interior to angle BAQ. This is a plane-separation (Pasch-type) fact that Euclid also takes for granted.
The case of Q on B's side is omitted; it follows by symmetry.
The inequality sign between BAQ and ABQ is ambiguous in the hand ('<.' or '>'). Mathematically it must be BAQ > ABQ.

results.what: Points on the perpendicular bisector of AB are equidistant from A and B; points off it are strictly closer to the endpoint on their own side.
results.modern_name: Perpendicular bisector theorem (locus characterization); equivalently, the half-planes determined by the perpendicular bisector are the Voronoi regions of A and B.
results.usually_credited_to: Classical Euclidean geometry (Euclid, Elements I, implicit in I.4, I.5, I.18-19, I.10-11; standard in school texts)

deep.surprise_reason: This is an elementary textbook theorem of Euclidean plane geometry with a standard Euclid-style proof. It may be a teaching or foundational exercise, possibly in another hand. Nothing here is non-standard.

checkable.asserts: With A=(0,1), B=(0,-1), C=(0,0), any R=(r,0) on the bisector satisfies AR^2 = BR^2.
QB^2 - QA^2 = 4y, so QB > QA exactly when Q=(x,y) lies on A's side (y > 0).
For Q=(0,q) with 0<q<1 (between C and A): QB = 1+q equals QA + 2CQ with QA = 1-q and CQ = q.
For Q=(0,q) with q>1 (beyond A): QB = QA + AB, with AB = 2.

transcription_corrections: The relation written before 'ABQ' in the last line appears in the image as '<.' (or an ambiguous sign), not clearly '>'. The intended and correct relation is BAQ > ABQ.
The insertion '= RAQ + ABQ' is written interlinearly above 'ABR also'. It reads 'BAR = RAQ + ABR = RAQ + ABQ'.
'Q' in 'Ein Punkt Q ausser' is an interlinear insertion above the line, as marked.
Line 2 of the proof reads 'Beweis. I. Ein Punkt in der Linie' with 'in' underlined; the 'E' of 'Ein' is overwritten.
